messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Nadia, an eighty-year-old widow and retired social worker of Middle Eastern descent, sat in the consultation room with her hands clasped tightly in her lap. She had come to therapy at the urging of her daughter, but what had finally pushed her through the door was a moment she could no longer outrun. A week earlier, while waiting for a routine blood test, the sharp, clean scent of antiseptic had hit her nostrils in the waiting room, and before she could brace herself, she was drowning. There was no image, no clear picture in her mind, but the feeling was absolute: the same crushing weight in her chest, the same cold dread, the same overwhelming grief that had seized her thirty years ago when her son, Amir, was diagnosed with leukemia. She could not see the hospital room, could not recall the doctor’s face, but she felt the terror as if it were happening in that moment, her body trembling, her breath short, her eyes filling with tears for no reason that the other patients could see.

The trauma itself had unfolded over eighteen months. Amir was twelve when the fevers started, then the bruising, then the diagnosis. Nadia had spent every day at his bedside, coordinating with doctors, translating medical jargon for her husband, who spoke little English, and trying to hold her family together. She had been the strong one, the one who made decisions, who signed consent forms, who told Amir he would be fine. But in the quiet hours of the night, when the IV drips beeped and the fluorescent lights hummed, she had felt a helplessness so profound it seemed to hollow her out from the inside. She had prayed, bargained, begged. And when Amir finally went into remission, Nadia had told herself the nightmare was over.

But it was not over. The nightmare had simply taken a different shape. Over the years, she had come to believe that she had acted in ways that went against everything she stood for. She had been so focused on survival that she had snapped at her husband, had missed her daughter’s school play, had once, in a moment of exhaustion, wished it would all just end. She carried these memories like stones in her chest, each one a proof that she had permanently changed for the worse. She was no longer the warm, patient woman she had once been. She was someone who could not stop bad things from happening, someone who had failed to protect her own child from the most basic threat of all.

The consequences of this belief had reshaped her life. She stopped going out, except for absolute necessities. The world outside her apartment felt unpredictable, dangerous. When friends called to invite her to dinner, she made excuses. When her daughter suggested a walk in the park, Nadia said she was tired. But the real reason was simpler and more terrifying: she could not bear to hear anyone talk about loss. A casual comment about a neighbor’s deceased husband, a news story about a child with cancer, even a friend reminiscing about a parent who had passed—these words hit her like physical blows, and she would feel the grief surge up, unbidden, as fresh as the day Amir was diagnosed. She had learned to scan conversations for danger, to steer topics away from anything resembling illness or death, and when she could not, she would push the thoughts out of her mind, shoving them down with a force that left her exhausted.

The avoidance had narrowed her world to a small, safe radius. She had not visited a hospital in years. When her own doctor recommended a physical examination, she cancelled the appointment and never rescheduled. She would cross the street to avoid passing a pharmacy, and the sound of an ambulance siren made her freeze in place, her heart hammering, until the noise faded. Her daughter had noticed, had grown worried, had finally insisted that something was wrong. Nadia had agreed to come to therapy not because she believed it would help, but because she was afraid of losing her daughter’s patience, afraid of being left alone entirely.

Now, sitting in the quiet office, she could smell nothing more threatening than coffee and paper. But she was certain that at any moment, the memory would force its way in again, without warning, and she would be back in that hospital room, helpless and grieving. What she hoped for, more than anything, was to find a way to stop feeling so much—or perhaps, to find a way to forgive herself for having felt it at all.
